did_you_know.text: Did you know? In the ancient world, a city gate was more than an entrance; it was a central place for meeting, trade, and public affairs.
Did you know? Washing a guest’s feet was part of hospitality because people traveled on dusty roads and usually wore sandals.
Did you know? Matzah is bread that has not had time to rise; it can be prepared quickly, fitting a story filled with urgency.
Did you know? In the Bible, the verb “to know” can also be a modest expression for sexual relations, not only for gaining knowledge.
Did you know? The men of Sodom portray Lot as an outsider who came to live among them, so they reject his criticism and authority.
Did you know? The biblical word sanverim is very rare; here it describes an impairment that prevents the men from seeing or finding the way.
Did you know? The verb “to hesitate” emphasizes that Lot struggles to leave even when the danger is immediate.
Did you know? The Hebrew word kikkar refers to a broad, level plain, so the story distinguishes the plain from the mountains where Lot is told to flee.
Did you know? The name Zoar is related to the Hebrew word for “small” or “little,” a wordplay that explains the city’s name within the story.
Did you know? Gofrit refers to a burning substance generally associated with sulfur, giving rise to the traditional phrase “fire and brimstone.”
Did you know? The Dead Sea region is rich in salt, so the image of a pillar of salt fits the story’s desert landscape, even without identifying a specific site.
Did you know? Comparing the smoke to smoke from a furnace creates an image of intense heat and thick smoke, not merely an ordinary fire.
Did you know? Lot’s rescue is also described as connected with God remembering Abraham, linking this chapter to Abraham’s prayer for Sodom.
